blocks.text: Replace a distributed transaction with a sequence of local transactions, each paired with a compensation that undoes it.

No single ACID transaction spans services, so a **saga** runs one local transaction per service. If step N fails, the saga executes the **compensating actions** for steps N-1 down to 1. Intermediate states are visible to others, so a saga gives atomicity of outcome but not isolation.

items: **Orchestration:** a coordinator tells each participant what to do.
**Choreography:** participants react to each other's events.
**Compensation:** a semantic undo (refund), not a rollback.

blocks.text: Compensations can fail too, and some steps cannot be undone (an email sent). Order them: compensatable steps first, then the pivot step, then retriable steps that are never undone.

walkthrough.note: A step pairs a forward action with its compensation. Defining both together makes it harder to add an action nobody knows how to undo.
The orchestrator runs steps in order and pushes each success onto a stack. On failure it pops the stack, so compensations run in reverse order of completion.
The workflow is data: reserve stock, hold points, charge the card, ship. The irreversible shipment is last. A declined card throws inside `charge`.
Run one: everything succeeds. Run two: the charge fails, the points hold and the reservation are undone in reverse order, and state returns to the start.

blocks.text: Booking a trip across flight, hotel and payment services.

Each service owns its database, so there is no shared transaction. The booking orchestrator reserves a seat, then a room, then charges the card. If the card is declined, it cancels the room and releases the seat. Each compensation is idempotent and retried until it succeeds, and the saga's state is persisted after each step so a restarted orchestrator resumes where it stopped.
Payoff: a failure at any point leaves every service consistent again, without locks held across the network.

lists.title: Use when
items: A business process spans services that own their data.
Locks or two-phase commit across services are impractical.
Every step has a meaningful business-level undo.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: One database can run the work in a local ACID transaction.
Steps need strict isolation, such as exact balances visible to all.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Dirty reads: other requests see intermediate state until compensation runs.
Every step and compensation must be idempotent and retryable.
Orchestrator state must be durable, or a crash strands the saga half done.
Lost updates: counter them with semantic locks (a PENDING state) or commutative updates.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: A saga for two steps in the same service and database.
Choreographed sagas across many services nobody can trace end to end.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Records and sealed events model saga steps and state cleanly.
Durable-execution engines such as Temporal persist progress for you.

rows.difference: Each step is a command with an undo. A saga adds the failure policy: on error it runs the undos in reverse order.
A unit of work gives ACID atomicity in one database. A saga offers eventual atomicity across services, using compensations instead of rollback.
Each saga step must update its data and send its next message atomically, which is what the outbox provides.
Messages and compensations can be redelivered, so each participant must apply them at most once in effect.
A saga's progress is a state machine, but State models one object's behavior. A saga coordinates several services and their undo.

exercises.prompt: Explain a Saga: why it exists, how failure is handled, and what it cannot give you.

modelAnswer.text: A saga splits a cross-service operation into local transactions, each with a compensating action. On failure, completed steps are compensated in reverse order, restoring consistency without distributed locks. It can't provide isolation: other requests may see intermediate states, and compensations must be idempotent.

keyPoints: Sequence of local transactions across services
Each step has a compensation, a semantic undo
On failure run compensations in reverse order
No isolation: intermediate states are visible
Steps and compensations must be idempotent and durable
